subject: korean
title: Name, job ... and country?
goal: Notice that two self-introduction cards do not contain the fact a question asks for, decide what is still missing, and ask for it in Korean.
thinking: Sufficiency of information
A name is a clue, not proof
Asking for the one missing fact
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks learners to read a card and answer from it. Here the question cannot be answered from the cards, and you must see why and ask.
prerequisites: Knows 이름, 학생, 선생님, 사람 and country names
material:
First day of class. Your teacher hands out two self-introduction cards (made up for this task).

[카드 1]
안녕하세요? 저는 수진이에요. 학생이에요.

[카드 2]
안녕하세요? 저는 마이클이에요. 선생님이에요.

The teacher points at card 1 and asks: "수진 씨는 한국 사람이에요?"

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: '수진 씨는 한국 사람이에요?' Using only the two cards, what is the best answer?

options.text: Yes. 수진 is a Korean name, so she is from Korea.
options.reveals: A name is a hint, not proof: people of many countries have Korean names, and Korean people have other names. Look for a sentence that names a country.

options.text: No. 학생 means she studies abroad, so she is not Korean.
options.reveals: 학생 only means 'student'. It says nothing about where she is from.

options.text: Not yet. The cards give her name and job, but no country.
Not yet. Card 1 has no name, so nobody can say.
options.reveals: The name is on the card: 수진. The missing piece is a different one.

steps.explain: Card 1 gives a name (수진) and a job (학생) but never a country. Card 2 does not help: it is about 마이클. The answer is 'unknown yet', and you need one more fact.
hints: List what each sentence on card 1 tells you: a name, a job ... anything else?
Ask yourself whether the cards contain any word for a country or '-사람'.

steps.prompt: Imagine 수진 adds ONE sentence to her card. Which added sentences would settle the teacher's question? Choose all that settle it (a 'yes' or a 'no' both count).

options.text: 저는 한국어를 공부해요.
options.reveals: Many people from many countries study Korean, so this does not tell her country.

options.text: 저는 호주 사람이에요.
저는 한국 사람이에요.
저는 커피를 좋아해요.
options.reveals: Liking coffee has nothing to do with a country.

steps.explain: A sentence with '-사람이에요' names the country. 호주 사람 answers 'no', 한국 사람 answers 'yes'. Studying Korean or liking coffee does not decide it.
hints: Look for the sentences that name a person's country, not a hobby or a study.
Test each sentence: after reading it, could you say 'yes' or 'no' for sure?

steps.prompt: Write your question to 수진 in Korean (polite -요 speech) to find out the missing fact.

checks.label: asks about her country or nationality

selfAssess: Does my question ask for the missing fact (the country) and not something the cards already say?
Is it polite (-요) and short enough to answer in one sentence?

badAnswers.why: Asks something the card already says.
The name is already on the card; the missing fact is the country.
Not a question; asks nothing.

steps.humanReview: Whether the question is natural and polite (e.g. 씨 after the name) needs a person.
hints: Decide first which fact is missing, then ask only about that.
End your sentence with a question form (-이에요? / -예요?).

rubric.full: Sees that the cards give no country and that a name does not prove one
rubric.none: Answers yes or no from the name or the job

rubric.full: Polite question that asks only for the missing fact
rubric.partial: Understandable but asks something already known
rubric.none: Not a question or agrees without asking

alternatives: '수진 씨는 한국 사람이에요?' is as good as 'which country' because the answer settles it.
Asking '어디에서 왔어요?' also targets the country.
hardCases: A learner may say a Korean-looking name is 'good evidence'. The task treats it as a hint only; a correct 'not yet' is based on the missing sentence.

cautions.language: Only 1급 words and the endings -이에요/예요, -아요/어요, -ㅂ니다; no romanization.
cautions.culture: Names do not decide nationality: people of any background may have a Korean or a foreign name. Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or pictures. Names, countries and ages are made up.

auto: Choice of what the cards do and do not say
The question form and a mention of country or 사람
human: Naturalness and politeness of the question

subject: korean
title: Rina's tag and Rina's words
goal: Check a spoken self-introduction against a name tag, find the one line whose fact is wrong, name the kind of mistake, and repair it.
thinking: Checking a text against a source
Separating a grammar error from a wrong fact
Repairing only what is wrong
differsFromPlain: Plain practice corrects the grammar of a sentence. Here every sentence is correct Korean, and the error is a fact that disagrees with another source.
prerequisites: Knows 선생님, 학생, 일본 사람 and -이에요/예요
material:
Rina is a visitor. She wears a name tag and introduces herself to the class.

[이름표]
이름: 리나
나라: 일본
직업: 선생님

She says the five lines below.

steps.prompt: Rina reads her self-introduction aloud. Compare it with her name tag. Exactly one line does not match the tag. Which line is it?
steps.explain: Line 4 says 학생이에요 ('I am a student'), but the tag says 선생님 (teacher). The Korean in line 4 is grammatically fine; the fact is wrong. Lines 2 and 3 match the tag, and lines 1 and 5 are greetings that carry no facts.
hints: Some lines are greetings and carry no facts. Mark the lines that do carry a fact.
Take the tag fact by fact (name, country, job) and find the line that says each one.

steps.prompt: What kind of mistake is the line you picked?

options.text: Wrong ending: it should be -예요, not -이에요.
options.reveals: The ending -이에요 is correct after a syllable with a final consonant (생). The sentence is grammatical.

options.text: The grammar is fine, but the fact disagrees with the name tag.
Too casual for a first meeting.
options.reveals: The ending -요 is already polite, so the register is fine.

options.text: 저는 should be 나는.
options.reveals: 저는 is the polite word for 'I' and fits a first meeting; 나는 would be the casual one.

steps.explain: A line can be correct Korean and still be wrong for the situation. Here the sentence is fine, but it does not match the tag.
hints: Read the line aloud as grammar only: does it break any rule?
Then compare its meaning, not its form, with the tag.

steps.prompt: Rewrite the wrong line in Korean so that it matches the name tag. Keep polite -요 speech.

checks.label: gives the job from the tag
does not repeat 'I am a student'

selfAssess: Does my line say the job that is on the tag?
Did I keep the ending polite?

badAnswers.why: Repeats the wrong fact.
Casual ending in a first-meeting introduction.
Says the country, not the job.

steps.humanReview: Whether the corrected line sounds natural in the speech needs a person.
hints: Put the correct job word from the tag into the same sentence pattern.
Check the ending: does the job word end in a consonant or a vowel?

rubric.full: Picks the line whose fact disagrees and says why
rubric.partial: Picks the right line without a reason
rubric.none: Picks a line with correct information or a greeting

rubric.full: Polite sentence with the job from the tag
rubric.none: Repeats the error or changes another fact

alternatives: Rewriting as '저는 학생이 아니에요. 선생님이에요.' is also fine.
Using 직업은 선생님이에요 also repairs the line.
hardCases: If the tag itself were misprinted, the line might be right. The task fixes the tag as the reliable source; in real life you would ask Rina.

cautions.language: Only 1급 words and the endings -이에요/예요, -아요/어요, -ㅂ니다; no romanization.
cautions.culture: Name tags and self-introductions often give name, country and job in that order. Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or pictures. Names, countries and ages are made up.

auto: The wrong line
The kind of mistake
The job word and a polite ending in the repair

subject: korean
title: One word, three scenes
goal: Read the same Korean word in three growing scenes, revise its meaning as the situation changes, say what decided it, and use it correctly yourself.
thinking: Meaning depends on context
Revising an interpretation with new information
Reading the line before
differsFromPlain: Plain practice lists one meaning of 아니에요. Here the meaning changes in each scene and you must justify it from the context.
material: Three short scenes between the classmates 하나 and 민수 (made up). They use polite -요 speech. Each scene is shown one at a time.

steps.prompt: The same word appears in three small scenes. Read each scene and decide what it means there before you see the next.

stages.info:
Scene 1. 하나 introduces her friend to 민수.

하나: 민수 씨, 이 사람은 지우 씨예요.
민수: 지우 씨는 선생님이에요?
하나: 아니에요.
stages.ask: What does 하나's 아니에요 mean here?

options.text: No, 지우 is not a teacher.
You're welcome.
options.reveals: Nobody has thanked her, so 'you're welcome' has no reason to be said.

options.text: I'm sorry.
options.reveals: Nobody has done anything wrong in this scene.

options.text: Never mind; it is okay.
options.reveals: Nothing needs forgiving here; 민수 asked a question.

stages.after: Answering a yes/no question, 아니에요 means 'no'.

stages.info:
Scene 2. Later, 민수 lends 하나 a pen.

하나: 고마워요!
민수: 아니에요.
stages.ask: What does 민수's 아니에요 mean now?

options.text: No, I did not lend you a pen.
options.reveals: He is holding out the pen. This reads the word the same way as in Scene 1 and ignores what 하나 just said.

options.text: It was nothing; you're welcome.
No, I am not 민수.
options.reveals: No one asked who he is.

options.text: I am sorry.
options.reveals: He has nothing to apologise for.

stages.after: After 고마워요, 아니에요 is a modest reply: 'It's nothing.' The same word now answers thanks, not a question.

stages.info:
Scene 3. In the hallway 민수 bumps into 하나's arm.

민수: 죄송해요!
하나: 아니에요.

options.text: No, you are not sorry.
options.reveals: Nothing in the scene says she doubts him; after an apology, the word gives comfort.

options.text: I'm not angry; it's all right.
No, I am not 하나.
options.reveals: No one asked who she is.

options.text: You're welcome.
options.reveals: He did not thank her; he apologised.

stages.after: After an apology, 아니에요 means 'It's fine, don't worry.' One word, three jobs: the line before it decides.

steps.reflect: Did your reading of 아니에요 change from scene to scene? What did you look at to decide each time?
hints: Before you choose, read the line just before the word.
Ask what the other person has just done: asked, thanked or apologised?

steps.prompt: Looking back at the three scenes, what decided the meaning of 아니에요 each time?

options.text: The sound of the word 아니에요.
options.reveals: The word was identical every time, so it cannot be what changed the meaning.

options.text: The line spoken just before it, and what had just happened.
Whether the speaker was a man or a woman.
options.reveals: Both men and women use the word in all three ways.

options.text: How loudly the word was said.
options.reveals: This task is about written text; the meaning here comes from the words before.

steps.explain: The word never changed. The meaning came from the previous line: a question (no), thanks (it's nothing) or an apology (it's fine).
hints: Compare what stayed the same and what changed across the three scenes.
Look at the thing that came right before the word each time.

steps.prompt: A classmate says '고마워요!' to you because you lent a pen. Reply in Korean (polite -요 speech) with a modest 'It's nothing'.
selfAssess: Does my reply play down the favour instead of repeating the thanks?
Is the ending polite?

badAnswers.why: Repeats the thanks instead of answering it.
A goodbye, not a reply to thanks.
An apology; nothing needs forgiving here.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reply feels natural for the classmate relationship needs a person.
hints: Think of the line you saw after 고마워요 in scene 2.
Keep the ending polite (-요); a short reply is fine.

rubric.full: Chooses a reasonable reading in each scene and sees that the word did not change
Modest, polite reply to thanks
rubric.none: Repeats thanks or answers something else

alternatives: '괜찮아요' is also a natural answer to 고마워요.
'천만에요' is a bit more formal but also correct.
hardCases: Some learners hear 아니에요 after thanks as a real 'no'. The scene (he lends the pen) shows it is modesty.

cautions.language: Only 1급 words and the endings -이에요/예요, -아요/어요, -ㅂ니다; no romanization.
cautions.culture: Modest replies to thanks and apologies are common in Korean everyday talk, but how often people use them varies. Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or pictures. Names, countries and ages are made up.

auto: Reasonable readings in each scene
Which clue decided the meaning
Reply contains a modest phrase and a polite ending

subject: korean
title: Who is younger? Only comparisons
goal: Turn four ordinary self-introductions that only compare ages into a rule, build several valid age sets, greet politely with one, and find what is true in all of them.
thinking: Comparisons are not numbers
Finding several solutions
What holds in every case
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads one age from one sentence. Here nobody says a number except 민아, so you must work with 'younger' and 'older' and see what is certain.
prerequisites: Has met -보다 (than); it is glossed under the material
material:
Four people meet in a Korean class (all made up). 민아 says her age. The others only compare.

민아: 저는 20살이에요.
하나: 저는 민아 씨보다 어려요. 지호 씨보다 나이가 많아요.
선생님: 저는 민아 씨보다 나이가 많아요.
(지호 says nothing about age.)

Words: 어려요 = is young (younger); 나이가 많아요 = is older; A보다 = than A.

steps.prompt: Hana says: '저는 민아 씨보다 어려요.' What does that tell you about Hana?

options.text: Hana is 19, so she is one year younger than 민아.
options.reveals: The sentence says 'younger' but no number. 19 is only one of many possible ages.

options.text: Hana is younger than 민아; the sentence gives no number.
Hana is older than 민아.
options.reveals: 어려요 means 'young'. -보다 means 'than', so Hana is younger, not older.

options.text: Hana and 민아 are the same age.
options.reveals: If they were the same age, nobody would say '어려요'.

steps.explain: '-보다 어려요' sets a comparison, not a number. Many ages fit.
hints: Find 보다 in the sentence and see which two people it connects.
Ask whether any number appears in her sentence.

steps.prompt: Everyone in the class is between 10 and 60. 민아 is 20. Build 3 different examples (j = 지호, h = 하나, t = 선생님) in which every sentence is true, and use a different age for 하나 in each.

constraints.fail: Ages are whole numbers.
Nobody in the class is under 10 or over 60.
하나 says she is younger than 민아, who is 20.
하나 says she is older than 지호.
선생님 says he or she is older than 민아, who is 20.

steps.explain: The sentences give only comparisons, so many ages fit: for example 12 < 15 < 20 < 35. Any numbers in the right order work.
hints: Put the four people in order from youngest to oldest first.
Pick 하나's age, then choose a younger 지호 and an older 선생님.
Check each Korean sentence against your numbers one by one.

because.prompt: Choose one of your examples. Write in Korean what 지호 says when he meets 선생님 for the first time: a polite greeting and his age.
selfAssess: Does the age I wrote match the 지호 number in my example?
Is the whole text polite?

badAnswers.why: Casual greeting and ending for a first meeting with a teacher.
Greets but gives no age.

because.humanReview: Whether the age matches the example and the text sounds natural needs a person.
hints: Start with the polite greeting you know from the first day of class.
Use your 지호 number plus 살 for the age.

steps.prompt: Which statement is true in EVERY correct example, not just in yours?

options.text: 하나 is two years younger than 민아.
options.reveals: The sentences only say 하나 is younger. In your examples the gap changes (15, 18, 19 ...).

options.text: 선생님 is older than 민아 by 10 years.
options.reveals: The sentences say 선생님 is older than 민아 but never say by how many years.

options.text: 선생님 is older than 지호.
지호 is older than 하나.
options.reveals: Check 하나's sentence again: 지호 is the younger one of the two.

steps.explain: 지호 < 하나 < 민아 (20) < 선생님, so 선생님 is older than 지호 in every example, even though no sentence says it directly.
hints: Write your three examples next to each other and see what never changes.
Follow the chain from the youngest to the oldest person.

rubric.full: Builds valid age sets and sees that the order is fixed but numbers are free
Polite greeting with an age

alternatives: Any ages in the right order are correct, e.g. 11 < 14 < 20 < 40.
Reading '나이가 많아요' as 'older' is the intended meaning.
hardCases: Some learners add that the youngest must greet first. That is a common custom, but it is not part of the sentences.

cautions.language: Only 1급 words and the endings -이에요/예요, -아요/어요, -ㅂ니다; no romanization.
cautions.culture: In Korea, age often shapes who uses which speech level; customs differ by place and person. Honorific and politeness norms vary by region, workplace, age and personal preference; this task reflects common standard-Korean usage, not a rule for every situation.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or pictures. Names, countries and ages are made up.

The greeting and an age with 살
human: Whether the age in the text matches the example

subject: korean
title: A self-introduction a stranger can use
goal: Write a three-sentence self-introduction for a given person, choosing the right form of 'to be' after each word, and answer a greeting in kind.
thinking: Giving a stranger the facts they need
Choosing a form by the last sound
Answering a greeting in kind
differsFromPlain: Plain practice fills in blanks in a model. Here you write your own sentences and the forms depend on the last sound of each word.
material:
You play 벤 (a made-up person) at your first Korean class. Here is his card.

[카드]
이름: 벤
나라: 호주
직업: 의사

The teacher is older than you.

steps.prompt: Your name is 벤 (it ends in a consonant, ㄴ). How do you say 'I am Ben'?

options.text: 저는 벤예요.
options.reveals: -예요 follows a syllable that ends in a vowel (e.g. 안나예요). 벤 ends in a consonant.

options.text: 저는 벤에요.
options.reveals: -에요 is not the form for names; use -이에요 or -예요.

options.text: 저는 벤이예요.
options.reveals: -이예요 is a common misspelling. The correct forms are -이에요 and -예요.

options.text: 저는 벤이에요.

steps.explain: After a final consonant use -이에요 (벤이에요, 사람이에요); after a vowel use -예요 (의사예요, 안나예요).
hints: Look at the last sound of 벤: does it end in a vowel or a consonant?
Remember the two forms of 'to be': one after a vowel, one after a consonant.

steps.prompt: Make your own introduction in Korean for this made-up person: 이름 벤 / 나라 호주 / 직업 의사. Greet first, then give name, country and job in 3 short sentences. Use polite speech.
selfAssess: Does my text give name, country and job?
Did I choose 이에요 or 예요 correctly after each word?
Could a stranger understand who I am from it?

modelAnswers.text: 안녕하세요? 저는 벤이에요. 호주 사람이에요. 의사예요.
안녕하세요, 제 이름은 벤이에요. 저는 호주 사람이에요. 의사예요.

badAnswers.text: 안녕하세요? 저는 벤예요. 호주 사람이에요. 의사예요.
badAnswers.why: Wrong form: 벤 ends in a consonant, so it is 벤이에요.

badAnswers.text: 안녕. 나는 벤이야. 호주 사람. 의사.
badAnswers.why: Casual style, not polite.
Name only; country and job are missing.

steps.humanReview: Whether the text sounds like a natural self-introduction needs a person.
hints: Start with the greeting you know, then add one fact per sentence.
Check each word before -이에요/예요: does it end in a consonant or a vowel?

steps.prompt: After your introduction, the teacher says '만나서 반가워요.' Reply in Korean (polite). Show that you feel the same.

checks.label: not negated (no 안 반가워요 / 반갑지 않아요)

selfAssess: Does my reply mirror the teacher's feeling?
Is it polite?

badAnswers.why: A goodbye, not a reply.
Thanks; the teacher did not give anything.
Means 'I don't know'.
Says the opposite: not glad to meet.

steps.humanReview: Natural use of 저도 and the warmth of the reply need a person.
hints: Read what the teacher says: what feeling does it express?
Reply so that the teacher hears you feel the same way, in polite speech.

rubric.full: Greeting, name, country and job in polite speech
Correct 이에요/예요 after every word

alternatives: 제 이름은 벤이에요 is as good as 저는 벤이에요.
Ending with -입니다 is also polite.
hardCases: Colloquial writing such as '벤에요' is heard in speech; this task treats the standard forms.

subject: korean
topic: Ordering food: menus with hidden conditions
title: Can we order the lunch set?
goal: Read a short menu sign, pick the facts that decide whether an order is possible, apply them to a real case, and ask the clerk a polite question about what is still available.
thinking: Telling relevant from irrelevant information
Checking that all conditions hold at once
Asking a clarifying question
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads the price off a sign. Here the sign hides conditions, and you must decide which facts to check before ordering.
prerequisites: Knows numbers + 시, 분 and 명
Knows 주문 and 세트 from the sign
material:
At a restaurant door you read this sign. The set is a Korean lunch special.

[점심 세트]
김치찌개 세트: 8,000원 (밥, 김치찌개, 음료)
시간: 12시 ~ 2시
두 명부터 주문해요.

steps.prompt: You and a friend want to eat the 김치찌개 세트 for lunch. Before you leave, which facts must you check against the sign to know whether you can order it? Choose all that apply.

options.text: The price per person (8,000원)
options.reveals: The price is printed on the sign, but it does not limit who may order or when.

options.text: What comes with the set (밥, 김치찌개, 음료)
options.reveals: This tells you what you get. It is not a rule for ordering.

options.text: How many people eat together
Which day of the week it is
options.reveals: The sign names no day.

options.text: What time you will arrive

steps.explain: The sign sets two conditions: the time (12 to 2) and the group size (two people or more). The drink, the money and the seat are not conditions.
hints: Read the sign line by line. Mark each line that sets a rule for ordering, and skip the lines that only list a price or an item.
Ask for each option: does the sign contain a rule about it?

steps.prompt: You and one friend arrive at the restaurant at 두 시 십 분 (2:10). Can you order the 김치찌개 세트?

options.text: Yes. You are two people, so the group condition is met.
options.reveals: Both conditions must be met. Check the time as well.

options.text: No. You are two people, but the set time ended at 2:00.
No. It is only for a single person, and you are two.
options.reveals: The sign says the opposite: it is for two people or more.

options.text: Yes. Lunch sets usually run a few minutes longer, so you can still order it.

differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to say where a place is from a picture. Here a route is already written, and you act as the checker: compare each line with the map and decide which lines fail and why.
prerequisites: Knows 왼쪽, 오른쪽, 옆, 에 있어요 and the place words on the map
material:
Mina writes a route for Jun. The street goes straight from the school gate.
Left side, in order from the gate: 은행 (bank), 편의점 (convenience store), 우체국 (post office).
Right side, in order from the gate: 병원 (hospital), 약국 (pharmacy), 카페 (café).

Mina's six lines are below. Some do not match the map.

steps.prompt: Pick one line that does NOT match the map.
steps.explain: Line 4 is wrong: the post office is beside the 편의점, not beside the bank (the 편의점 is between them). Line 5 is wrong: the hospital is on the right side. Lines 1, 2, 3 and 6 match the map.
hints: Check the lines one at a time against the map: first the side, then the neighbour.
For each line with 옆, name the two neighbours of that place on its side of the street.

steps.prompt: Which of these sentences is TRUE for the map?

options.text: 약국은 편의점 옆에 있어요.
options.reveals: The pharmacy and the convenience store are on opposite sides of the street; 옆 does not cross the street.

options.text: 병원은 카페 옆에 있어요.
options.reveals: The pharmacy is between the hospital and the café; 옆 means the very next place.

options.text: 약국은 카페 옆에 있어요.
은행은 우체국 옆에 있어요.
options.reveals: The convenience store is between the bank and the post office; being on the same side is not enough for 옆.

steps.explain: 옆 means the very next place on the same side. The pharmacy and the café are neighbours on the right side.
hints: For each sentence find both places on the map, then count the places between them.
Also check which side of the street each place is on.

steps.prompt: Rewrite line 4 in Korean so that it matches the map.

checks.label: names the right neighbour with 옆 (or 다음)
does not say the post office is next to the bank

selfAssess: Does my sentence name the place that is really next to the post office?
Does it still end like Mina's other lines (…에 있어요)?

badAnswers.why: Same mistake: the bank is not next to the post office.
Does not give the right neighbour.

steps.humanReview: Whether another correct description (for example with 끝 or 세 번째) is also acceptable.
hints: Look at the map: which place is right beside the post office?
Keep the shape of the other lines: place + 은/는 + place + 옆에 있어요.

rubric.full: Picks line 4 or 5 and says why it contradicts the map
rubric.partial: Picks a wrong line without a reason

rubric.full: Says 옆 means the very next place on the same side
rubric.none: Treats 옆 as anywhere on the street

alternatives: Line 5 can also be fixed: '병원은 오른쪽에 있어요.'
'우체국은 맨 끝에 있어요' (맨 끝 = very end) is also true but goes beyond 1급 words.
hardCases: In daily speech 옆 is sometimes used loosely for 'near'; the task uses the strict 'next one' reading.

cautions.language: Only simple location sentences. 왼쪽/오른쪽 are viewed from someone walking from the school gate.
cautions.culture: Korean streets often have a row of shops on each side, so 'next to' is a common way to give directions.
cautions.accessibility: The map is given in words; no picture is needed. Colour is not used.

auto: Picking a line that contradicts the map
Choice of the true sentence
Rewritten line names 우체국 and 편의점 with 옆 and avoids the bank claim
human: Other valid ways to describe the position

subject: korean
topic: Places in a town: 번, 옆, 오른쪽
title: Three notes, more than one street
goal: Build several different street arrangements that fit short Korean notes, and see that the notes do not decide one answer.
thinking: Several answers can fit the same conditions
Reading each condition exactly
Not generalising from one example
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives one picture and asks where a place is. Here the notes allow several streets, so you must test your own arrangements against every note and notice what is still undecided.
prerequisites: Knows Sino-Korean numbers 일 to 오, 번, 옆, 오른쪽
material:
A short street has 5 spots in a row, numbered 1 to 5 from the LEFT end. The 은행 (bank), the 병원 (hospital) and the 약국 (pharmacy) each stand on one spot. No two share a spot, and two spots stay empty. Jun's notes:

1. 병원은 은행 오른쪽에 있어요.
2. 약국은 병원 옆에 있어요.
3. 은행은 일 번이 아니에요.

(오른쪽 = somewhere to the right, not necessarily right next to it.)

steps.prompt: Ignore the bank for a moment. The 병원 is on spot 4. By note 2, where can the 약국 be?

options.text: On spot 3 only
options.reveals: 옆 means either neighbour, left or right.

options.text: On spot 2 or spot 5
options.reveals: Spot 2 is two steps away; 옆 means the very next spot.

options.text: On spot 5 only
options.reveals: 옆 means either neighbour, left or right.

options.text: On spot 3 or spot 5

steps.explain: 옆 means a next spot, on either side: spot 3 or spot 5.
hints: Draw five spots in a row and mark spot 4. Look at the spots that touch it.
Read note 2 again and check whether it names a side.

steps.prompt: Find 3 different arrangements that fit all three notes. b = spot of the 은행, h = spot of the 병원, p = spot of the 약국.

constraints.fail: Each spot must be a whole number from 1 to 5.
Two places share a spot.

constraints.ok: 병원 is to the right of 은행 (note 1).
constraints.fail: Note 1: 병원 must be to the right of 은행, so its number is bigger.
Note 2: 약국 must be on the spot right beside 병원.
Note 3: 은행 is not 일 번.

steps.explain: For example: bank 2, hospital 3, pharmacy 4; or bank 2, hospital 4, pharmacy 5; or bank 3, hospital 5, pharmacy 4. There are six arrangements in all. The notes give limits, not one exact street.
hints: Start with note 3 and note 1: choose a spot for the bank, then a spot to its right for the hospital.
Then place the pharmacy right beside the hospital on a free spot.
Check each note one by one for your row.

because.prompt: Take ONE of your arrangements. Write one Korean sentence (polite -요) that says where the 약국 is, using 옆.

checks.label: names the neighbour directly before 옆 (병원 옆 / 은행 옆)

selfAssess: Does my sentence match the row I built?
Did I name the real neighbour of the 약국 in my row?

modelAnswers.text: 병원 옆에 약국이 있어요. 약국은 사 번이에요.

badAnswers.why: No neighbour and no 옆.
Does not describe the 약국.
Word order is wrong: the neighbour must come before 옆.

because.humanReview: Whether the named neighbour is the real neighbour in the learner's own row (the checker cannot see the row).
hints: Look at your row: which place stands right beside the 약국?
Use the pattern: place + 은/는 + place + 옆에 있어요.

steps.prompt: Jun's friend looks only at the row bank 2, hospital 3, pharmacy 4 and says: 'So the 약국 must be on spot 4.' What is true about the three notes?

options.text: The notes fit only one row, so the 약국 is on spot 4.
options.reveals: The notes fit six rows. Spot 4 is only one of the possible places.

options.text: The notes fit several rows, but the 약국 must always be next to the 은행.
options.reveals: Only two of the six rows have the 약국 next to the 은행; no note says so.

options.text: The notes fit several rows, and the 약국 can be on spot 3, 4 or 5.
The notes fit several rows, but the 약국 can only be on spot 3 or 4.
options.reveals: Spot 5 also works, for example bank 2, hospital 4, pharmacy 5.

options.text: The notes fit several rows, but the 약국 must always be on spot 5.
options.reveals: Some rows have the 약국 on spot 3 or 4, so it is not always on spot 5.

steps.explain: The notes fit six rows and the pharmacy is on spot 3 in one row, on spot 4 in three rows and on spot 5 in two rows. One example is never enough to say what must be true.
hints: Look at the rows you built: do they all have the 약국 on the same spot?
A statement with 'must' needs to be true in every row that fits.

rubric.full: Three different rows that pass every note
Says the notes allow several spots for the 약국
rubric.partial: Notices more than one row but not what varies

alternatives: Any three of the six are accepted.
hardCases: Some learners read 오른쪽 as 'right next to'. The material states that it means 'somewhere to the right'.

cautions.language: Sino-Korean numbers with 번 (일 번, 이 번 ...) are used for spot numbers.
cautions.culture: Numbering shop spots in a row is common on Korean shopping streets.
cautions.accessibility: The street is described in words and numbers; no picture is needed.

auto: Every built row is checked against all notes
Number of different rows
Choice about what the notes decide
Presence of 약국, 옆, a neighbour and a polite ending
human: Whether the sentence matches the learner's own row

subject: korean
topic: Asking the way: subway station and exits
title: Are they in the same place yet?
goal: Revise your judgement about whether two friends are in the same place as more details arrive, then write the message that fixes it.
thinking: How much a place name really pins down
Revising a judgement when new information arrives
Giving an exact meeting place
differsFromPlain: Plain practice names places on a subway line. Here the same two sentences become more exact in three steps, and you decide after each step whether 'same place' is already true.
prerequisites: Knows 역, 출구, Sino-Korean numbers 일 to 오
material: Hana and Jun are going to meet at the subway. They talk on the phone. Read each part and decide what you can say so far.

steps.prompt: Read each part and choose the most reasonable reading of where they are.
hints: Decide using only the lines you have read so far.
Ask yourself: is there still more than one place that fits both sentences?
steps.reflect: A place word can fit many places at first. Each new detail (the station name, then the exit) makes the place smaller. Meeting works only when the detail is exact enough.

stages.info:
하나: 준, 지금 어디예요?
준: 저는 역에 있어요.
하나: 저도 역에 있어요!
stages.ask: Are Hana and Jun in the same place?

options.text: Yes. Both are at the station, so they are together.
options.reveals: Each only said 역 (a station). There are many stations in a city.

options.text: No. They said the same word, so they must be at different stations.
options.reveals: The same word does not show different stations; the lines simply do not say which station.

options.text: Maybe. Both said 역, but there are many stations.
Yes. Hana said 저도, so she is at Jun's station.
options.reveals: 저도 means 'me too' (also at a station), not 'at the same one'.

stages.after: '역' only says what kind of place. Without a name, we cannot know whether it is the same station.

stages.info:
하나: 무슨 역이에요?
준: 시청역이에요.
하나: 저도 시청역이에요!

options.text: They are in the same station, but we cannot yet say they stand in the same spot.
They are on different lines, so they must be far away.
options.reveals: Both said 시청역. Nothing here shows different stations.

options.text: They are together at exactly the same spot.
options.reveals: A station can be big with several exits; the same station is not yet the same spot.

options.text: We still know nothing, because 시청역 can be anywhere.
options.reveals: The station name 시청역 does fix the station; what is open is the spot inside it.

stages.after: The station is the same, but a big station has several exits. The exact spot is still open.

stages.info:
준: 저는 이 번 출구 앞이에요.
하나: 어? 저는 일 번 출구 앞이에요.

options.text: They are together; the exit does not matter.
options.reveals: Exit 1 and exit 2 can be far apart on the street.

options.text: They are in different stations.
options.reveals: Both said 시청역; only the exits are different.

options.text: They are at the same exit; 일 and 이 sound alike.
options.reveals: 일 (1) and 이 (2) are different numbers, so they said different exits.

options.text: Same station, but at different exits. They are not in the same spot yet.

stages.after: Both sentences are true at the same time: one station, two exits. They still have to choose one exit.

steps.prompt: Now Hana and Jun need to meet. Who should walk to the other person's exit?

options.text: Either one; they only need to agree on one exit
Hana, because Jun spoke first
options.reveals: Who spoke first does not decide it.

options.text: Neither, because they are in the same station and can already see each other
options.reveals: A big station has several exits; the same station is not the same spot.

options.text: Both should stay where they are and wait
options.reveals: If both wait at different exits, they never meet.

steps.explain: Either can walk, or both can go to a third exit. What matters is that they name one exit and agree on it.
hints: Is there any rule that says one of them must move?
What would make both of them end up at the same exit?

steps.prompt: Write Jun's next message in Korean (polite -요) so they will meet. Name one exit.

checks.label: names exit 1 or exit 2 (… 번 출구)

selfAssess: Does my message give one exit only?
Would Hana know exactly where to stand?

modelAnswers.text: 하나, 이 번 출구 앞에서 기다려요.

badAnswers.why: Names the station but no exit; that is what went wrong.
Does not say where to meet and names no exit.
There is no exit 3; only exit 1 and exit 2 exist.

badAnswers.text: 일 번 출구에서 만나요 이 번 출구에서도 만나요.
badAnswers.why: Names two exits, so the place is still not exact.

steps.humanReview: Whether the message is natural and unambiguous (for example, whether a plan to move is clear).
hints: What was the detail that was missing in the end?
Choose one of the two exits and put its number into the place of the meeting.

rubric.full: Moves from 'maybe' to 'same station' to 'different exits' with reasons
rubric.partial: Changes the answer but without a reason

rubric.full: Message names one exit and is polite

alternatives: At stage 2, 'same station, maybe different exits' is the best reading, but a learner who says 'probably together' should still read the next stage.
Any exit number may be chosen in the last step.
hardCases: Stations also have names with line numbers (이 호선) that are not used here.

cautions.language: Only 역 and 출구 plus numbers. 일 번 / 이 번 are Sino-Korean numbers.
cautions.culture: Korean subway stations are large and have numbered exits; meeting at 'N번 출구' is a very common habit.
cautions.accessibility: No pictures needed; all information is text.

auto: Stage choices are compared with reasonable readings
Choice about who moves
Exit number and polite ending present
human: Naturalness and clarity of the message

subject: korean
topic: Simple transport: reading a bus sign
title: What the bus sign really says
goal: Decide which statements about a bus are supported by a sign, apply the sign to a particular day and time, and correct a claim that goes too far.
thinking: A general claim fails when one case breaks it
Matching a claim to the evidence (a sign) day by day
Correcting a claim with a precise statement
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads a timetable aloud. Here friends make claims about it and you judge which ones the sign supports, then apply it to one morning and correct a claim.
prerequisites: Knows days of the week, 버스, 있어요/없어요, clock times in digits
material:
The sign at the bus stop in front of the hospital:

10번 버스
월~금  06:00 ~ 22:00
토  08:00 ~ 20:00
일  없어요

(월~금 = Monday to Friday.) Four friends talk about bus 10.

steps.prompt: Which friends' sentences does the sign support? Choose all.

options.text: 민수: 십 번 버스는 매일 있어요.
options.reveals: The sign says 일 없어요, so there is no bus on Sunday.

options.text: 수지: 십 번 버스는 일요일에 없어요.
하나: 십 번 버스는 토요일 아침 여섯 시에 있어요.
options.reveals: On Saturday the first bus is at 08:00, not at 06:00.

options.text: 준: 십 번 버스는 수요일 저녁 아홉 시에 있어요.

steps.explain: 수지 is right (Sunday: 없어요). 준 is right (Wednesday 21:00 is between 06:00 and 22:00). 민수's 매일 is broken by Sunday, and 하나 uses the weekday start time for Saturday.
hints: Check each sentence against the line of the sign for that day.
For a time, compare it with the start and the end times of that line. Remember 아침 여섯 시 = 06:00 and 저녁 아홉 시 = 21:00.

steps.prompt: It is Saturday, 7:00 in the morning (아침 일곱 시). Jun wants to take bus 10 to the hospital. What should he do?

options.text: Take it now, because buses start at 06:00
options.reveals: 06:00 is the weekday start. Saturday has its own times.

options.text: Use another way, because there is no bus today
options.reveals: Only Sunday has no bus.

options.text: Wait until Monday, because buses do not run on weekends
options.reveals: Saturday has a bus from 08:00.

options.text: Wait one hour, because Saturday buses start at 08:00

steps.explain: The Saturday line says 08:00 ~ 20:00, so at 07:00 there is no bus yet but there will be in one hour.
hints: Find the line for Saturday first.
Compare 07:00 with the start time of that line.

steps.prompt: 민수 said: '십 번 버스는 매일 있어요.' Write one Korean sentence (polite -요) that corrects him.

checks.label: says there is no bus (없어요 / 안 와요 / 안 다녀요)
does not say there is a bus on Sunday

selfAssess: Does my sentence say which day breaks his claim?
Is my sentence true for the sign?

badAnswers.why: Repeats the wrong claim.
Saturday has a bus; the day is wrong.

steps.humanReview: Whether the correction is clear and polite.
hints: Find the line of the sign that does not fit '매일'.
Name that day and use 없어요.

rubric.full: Chooses 수지 and 준 and says why 민수 and 하나 fail
Names Sunday and says there is no bus
rubric.partial: Says the claim is wrong without the day

alternatives: '일요일에는 버스가 안 다녀요' is also a natural correction.
A learner may add the Saturday times; that is fine.
hardCases: Real timetables use 'every 10 minutes' etc.; this sign gives only the first and last time.

cautions.language: Numbers: 10번 on the sign, 십 번 in speech. Clock times on the sign are in digits; the spoken forms (여섯 시) appear in the options.
cautions.culture: Some Korean bus lines run less on Saturday and not on Sunday or holidays; signs and apps show the exact days.
cautions.accessibility: The sign is written as plain text; no colours or symbols carry meaning.

auto: Which claims the sign supports
Choice for Saturday 07:00
Sunday and no-bus wording present, no 'bus on Sunday' claim
human: Clarity and politeness of the correction

subject: korean
title: Sora's claim about Minsu's mornings
goal: Check a short claim about a weekly routine against the note it comes from, find the sentence that is the real evidence, and correct the claim with the days and times that belong together.
thinking: Testing a general claim ('every day') against the evidence
Finding the sentence that settles it
Keeping each time attached to the right days
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read a daily routine and answer 'what time does he get up?'. Here a classmate makes a claim that sounds natural, and you must check whether the note really supports it before you correct it.
prerequisites: Knows days of the week, 시 with native numbers, and -아요/어요
Knows 매일 (every day); it is glossed in the hints
material:
Minsu wrote about his week for his Korean class. His classmate Sora read it and made a claim.

민수의 일주일
월요일부터 금요일까지 학교에 가요.
그래서 아침 여섯 시에 일어나요.
토요일과 일요일에는 열 시에 일어나요.
그리고 저녁 열한 시에 자요.

소라: 민수는 매일 여섯 시에 일어나요.

steps.prompt: Does Minsu's note support Sora's claim? (매일 = every day)

options.text: Yes. The note says he gets up at six, and the note is about his week.
options.reveals: The note is about his whole week, but it gives more than one time. A claim about every day needs every day to fit.

options.text: No. The note gives two different get-up times for different days.
Yes. 그래서 shows six o'clock is his rule for the whole week.
options.reveals: 그래서 gives the reason for six o'clock (school), so it only covers the days that have school.

options.text: We cannot tell. The note says nothing about Saturday and Sunday.
options.reveals: The note does say something about Saturday and Sunday: look at which sentence names them.

steps.explain: The note names two groups of days: Monday to Friday (six o'clock, because of school) and Saturday and Sunday (ten o'clock). 'Every day at six' only matches the first group.
hints: Make a small list: which days does each sentence talk about?
Put Sora's time next to every time you find in the note.
Ask: if one day had a different time, would '매일' still be true?

steps.prompt: Which sentence of the note is the strongest evidence against Sora's claim?

options.text: 월요일부터 금요일까지 학교에 가요.
options.reveals: This sentence names the school days, but it says nothing that contradicts 'six o'clock'. It is the reason for the next sentence.

options.text: 그래서 아침 여섯 시에 일어나요.
options.reveals: This sentence supports Sora for Monday to Friday. Evidence against the claim must show a different time.

options.text: 토요일과 일요일에는 열 시에 일어나요.
그리고 저녁 열한 시에 자요.
options.reveals: Going to bed is a different habit. It does not change when he gets up.

steps.explain: Only this sentence names other days with another get-up time (ten o'clock). A claim about 'every day' fails as soon as one day has a different time.
hints: Evidence against a claim has to say something different from the claim.
Look for the sentence about getting up (일어나요) on other days.

steps.prompt: Rewrite Sora's sentence so that it matches the note. Say which days go with which time. Write in Korean (English is also accepted).

checks.label: Monday-Friday (school days) are paired with six o'clock
Saturday-Sunday (weekend) are paired with ten o'clock

selfAssess: Does my sentence give two groups of days?
Is each time next to the right days (six for school days, ten for the weekend)?

modelAnswers.text: 민수는 월요일부터 금요일까지 여섯 시에 일어나요. 토요일과 일요일에는 열 시에 일어나요.
He gets up at 6 on weekdays and at 10 on Saturday and Sunday.

badAnswers.why: Repeats the claim: no second group of days and no ten o'clock.

badAnswers.text: 월요일부터 금요일까지 열 시에 일어나요. 토요일과 일요일에는 여섯 시에 일어나요.
badAnswers.why: Both times are mentioned but they are attached to the wrong days.

steps.humanReview: Whether the Korean sentence is natural, and cases where the learner pairs times and days in an unusual order or style that the pattern checks cannot read.
hints: Your sentence needs two parts, one for each group of days.
Check the note again: which time belongs to Monday to Friday, and which to Saturday and Sunday?
Use the same ending as the note (-아요/어요).

rubric.full: Sees that the claim does not fit and points to the weekend sentence as the evidence
rubric.partial: Sees that the claim is wrong but cannot say which sentence shows it

rubric.full: Two groups of days, each with the right time
rubric.partial: Only one group, or the times are mixed up

alternatives: 평일 / 주말 are not in the note but are accepted as a summary of the days.
A correction in English is accepted at this level.
hardCases: If a learner writes '보통 여섯 시에 일어나요', the claim is softened with 보통 (usually). It is better, but it still hides the weekend time.

cautions.language: Only -아요/어요 and native numbers for clock hours (여섯 시, 열 시). 매일 is explained in the hints and options.
cautions.culture: Waking later on the weekend is shown here as one person's habit, not as a rule about Korean people.
cautions.accessibility: All material is plain text; no pictures, colours or sounds are needed. Times are written in words and digits.

auto: Choice of verdict and of the evidence sentence
Each time paired with the right days in the rewrite

subject: korean
title: Hana's diary: when did it happen?
goal: Find the diary sentences where the time word and the verb ending point to different times, say what is wrong, and fix one sentence in two possible ways.
thinking: Matching time words with verb endings (past, present, future)
Explaining a mismatch, not only spotting it
Repairing a sentence in more than one way
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to change a verb into the past. Here the verbs are already conjugated, and you must notice that two sentences contradict their own time word.
prerequisites: Has met -았어요/-었어요 (past) and -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (future); they are explained in the hints
material:
Hana writes a short diary on Wednesday morning. Two of her sentences have a time word that does not fit the verb ending.

steps.prompt: Pick one line where the time word and the verb ending point to different times.
